body.text: North Korea under Kim Jong Un presents a striking economic paradox. Despite closer economic and military cooperation with Russia, renewed trade with China, and signs of economic recovery, the country remains constrained by international sanctions, structural inefficiencies, and an economic system incapable of delivering sustained improvements in living standards. Meanwhile, the leadership continues to prioritize military development and centralized political control over fundamental economic transformation.

Although informal markets and private economic activities have progressively expanded, the state has resisted introducing comprehensive market-oriented economic reforms. Instead, successive generations of the Kim family have sought to preserve the socialist system established by Kim Il Sung, despite its persistent failure to deliver the workers’ welfare state it promised.

For North Korea, meaningful economic reform would require considerably more than so-called “improvements” (개선) or “enhancements” (강화). It would entail fundamental changes to the ownership of the means of production, including the recognition of private property and enterprise. It would also require replacing the country’s confrontational foreign policy with more cooperative international relations, relaxing totalitarian political controls, and allowing greater freedom of economic activity.

Crucially, introducing market-oriented reform would also challenge the ideological foundations of the North Korean socialist system. Recognizing private property and private enterprise would inevitably allow the emergence of different economic interests and social classes, contradicting the socialist objective of eliminating class divisions and the associated principle of class struggle. These principles, rooted in Marxist-Leninist doctrine and subsequently incorporated into the regime’s ruling ideology of Juche, remain fundamental to the political and ideological legacy of Kim Il Sung, the founding leader of North Korea.
Market-oriented reform would therefore require not simply economic restructuring, but also a fundamental reconsideration of the ideological principles upon which the regime has built its legitimacy.

The Juche ideology established by Kim Il Sung maintains that the socialist system represents a superior form of political and economic organization, capable of creating an affluent workers’ welfare state free from exploitation and oppression. Introducing fundamental market-oriented reform would amount to acknowledging that this system has failed to fulfill its promises. It would therefore require Kim Jong Un to renounce the ideological and institutional legacy of his grandfather.

However, Kim Jong Un’s political legitimacy derives from his position as the successor to Kim Il Sung and the defender of his revolutionary and ideological legacy. Kim Jong Un’s authority rests on the claim that he is continuing and advancing the socialist system established by his grandfather, whose achievements remain central to the regime’s identity. Renouncing that system would undermine the foundations of Kim Jong Un’s own legitimacy.

Yet this constraint also presents an opportunity. Sustained economic development and improvements in living standards could provide Kim Jong Un with an alternative basis for political legitimacy, shifting the foundations of his authority from revolutionary inheritance to economic performance.

There are other obstacles. Market-oriented reform requires access to international markets, foreign investment, technology, and financial resources. North Korea cannot realistically attract sustained foreign investment while pursuing a confrontational foreign policy characterized by military provocations and nuclear threats. Economic reform would therefore require peaceful coexistence, improved diplomatic relations, and a negotiated settlement of the nuclear issue. This would also challenge Kim Jong Un’s reliance on nuclear weapons as a source of domestic political legitimacy.

As Deng Xiaoping recognized, “No country can develop by closing its doors.” Economic development cannot be achieved in isolation; it requires engagement with international markets, access to foreign capital, and the adoption of advanced technologies and expertise. China’s subsequent experience demonstrated that economic opening could generate rapid development without abandoning Communist Party rule.

For North Korea, however, such opening would present two significant political risks: exposing the regime’s failures and weakening its control over the population, while also implicitly acknowledging the failure of its economic system in its historical competition with South Korea.

Greater openness would expose the corruption, institutional failures, political privileges, and human rights abuses that the regime has sought to conceal. Such revelations could undermine public confidence in the leadership. Furthermore, relaxing restrictions on movement and communication with the outside world could encourage large-scale defections, particularly to South Korea. Both developments would weaken the regime’s ability to maintain control over its population.

Since the division of the Korean Peninsula, North and South Korea have pursued competing political and economic systems: socialism in the North and a market-oriented system in the South. South Korea’s subsequent economic transformation has produced an enormous disparity in living standards between the two countries. For the Kim family, adopting market-oriented reform would therefore amount to acknowledging that its economic system has lost this historical competition.

Despite these obstacles, the economic reality within North Korea has fundamentally changed. The socialist system established by Kim Il Sung has been progressively displaced by marketization from below. Informal markets and private economic activity now sustain much of the population, while central planning and the state distribution system have substantially deteriorated. The resulting distorted economic system bears little resemblance to the socialist welfare state promised by the regime’s founding ideology.

This contradiction increasingly undermines the ideological foundations of the Kim family’s legitimacy. The population depends on economic activities that the socialist system was never designed to accommodate, yet these activities remain without adequate legal recognition or protection. The essential task is therefore to formalize the market economy that has already emerged by recognizing private property, legitimizing private enterprise, and establishing the institutions necessary to mobilize savings and investment for productive development.

Market-oriented reform consequently offers Kim Jong Un an opportunity to establish a new source of legitimacy based on economic performance and improvements in living standards, rather than relying exclusively on his grandfather’s revolutionary legacy. It would also provide the economic foundations necessary for North Korea’s survival as a sovereign state beyond his own tenure.

Kim Jong Un thus faces a fundamental choice. Continuing to preserve the existing system will perpetuate its economic dysfunction and deepen the contradiction between ideological promises and economic reality. Introducing fundamental market-oriented reform would challenge the foundations of his current legitimacy, but sustained economic development offers the only viable means of establishing a new one and securing North Korea’s long-term survival.
